entries.text: Inspired by the spring assisted hand orthosis, can have a spring that helps flexion instead of extension, and it would be best if it led to static balancing, canceling out the force of the “pressure”/rubber bands on back.

summary.title: Passive hydraulic grip assistance for EVA gloves
summary.problem: Pressurized EVA gloves resist finger movement, so astronauts work harder to close their hands and tire faster. Repetitive gripping is among the most fatiguing parts of a spacewalk, and Artemis missions will ask for more EVA hours than Apollo did.
summary.approach: A glove with rubber bands on the back stands in for a pressurized glove. A passive hydraulic system — syringes, fluid-filled tubing and tendon strings — is added to assist finger flexion without motors or electronics. Hand performance and perceived effort are compared with a bare hand, the glove with bands, and the glove with bands plus the assist.
summary.goal: Design, build and test a passive hydraulic prototype that assists finger flexion, and find out whether it reduces the effort to close the hand.

S.text: Problem is well motivated with NASA sources, including 2026 Artemis workload research.
Clear grasp of the SSRG and a real niche: a simpler, unpowered alternative.
Three-condition design mirrors the Madden et al. study, so results are easy to compare.
Cheap, available parts make quick iteration easy; spending is well under budget.
Already names leaks, air and weak force as risks.

W.text: The energy source and timing of the assist aren’t defined yet.
Pulling on syringes caps force and invites bubbles.
No hypothesis or target to call it a success.
Rubber band resistance isn’t measured or standardized.
Parts list is missing string, the grip device and fittings; glove cost is off.
Building doesn’t start until late fall, close to winter break.

O.text: Aim to cancel the glove’s stiffness (static balancing) instead of overpowering it.
A stopcock in the line gives a passive grip lock for holding tasks.
Rehab devices (tenodesis orthoses, body-powered prosthetics) offer tested passive ideas.
Tune the bands to NASA’s published grip-strength figures.
Bench tests give clean data independent of how hard he squeezes.

T.text: The measurable effect may be small; a clear null result is still a valid outcome.
Always-on assist could make opening the hand harder.
Leaks and air can make results vary between sessions.
Schedule slip could squeeze the testing window.

sugg.text: Decide where the assist energy comes from
sugg.why: A passive system can only redirect or store energy. If extending the same hand drives the input, it pulls the fingers closed at the same moment you’re opening them.

sugg.text: Push the syringes, never pull them
sugg.why: Suction tops out around 1 atmosphere and air comes out of solution. Mount the output so a pushing plunger pulls the string.

sugg.text: Use Luer-lock syringes, barb adapters and clamps
sugg.why: Otherwise most of the time goes to chasing leaks.
A one-finger rig before winter break leaves spring for improving it.
Later, a floating pulley (whiffletree) lets several fingers close around odd shapes.

sugg.text: Replace open jump rings with sewn loops or tubing guides
sugg.why: Anchor each string firmly at the fingertip.
Stretch in the string eats up assist travel.

sugg.text: Calibrate the bands with a scale
sugg.why: Aim for grip with the glove at about 50–60% of bare-hand, close to NASA’s pressurized-glove numbers.
Force to close the glove at a few positions, assist on vs. off.

sugg.text: Test over several days and vary the order
sugg.why: Note in the write-up that he is the only test subject.

sugg.text: Try a stopcock as a grip lock
sugg.why: Close the valve and the fluid holds the grip — a passive version of the SSRG’s hold mode.
The SSRG made opening the hand harder; worth knowing if this design does the same.
Typos (“cold” for “could”), a duplicated sentence, and matching the parts list to the proposal.

glossary.def: A syringe tip with screw threads, so tubing fittings twist on and stay locked under pressure.
A smooth, tapered syringe tip that fittings simply push onto. Cheaper, but connections can pop off under pressure.
A fitting with ridges (barbs) that grip the inside of flexible tubing, used to connect tubing to a syringe tip.
A small valve with three ports and a turning lever that can open, close or redirect flow between them.
Pushing trapped air bubbles out of a fluid line. Air squeezes, so bubbles make the system feel spongy and lose travel.
The ratio of two plunger areas. Output force changes by this ratio, and output travel changes by its inverse.
How hard the fluid pushes on the inside of the tubing, in pounds per square inch. The project tubing is rated to 90 psi.
Drag from a syringe’s rubber plunger seal sliding along the barrel. It uses up some of the force before it reaches the output.
Pushing a plunger raises fluid pressure with no hard limit. Pulling creates suction, which can never exceed about 1 atmosphere (14.7 psi) and lets dissolved air bubble out.
A balancing linkage that splits one pull among several strings, so each finger can stop at a different point when wrapping around an object.
Adding a spring or similar element that cancels another stiffness, so a joint feels close to neutral in every position.
Closing a valve so the trapped fluid can’t move, which holds the connected parts in place without continued effort.
Moving a joint by pulling a string routed along it, the way tendons move fingers. The SSRG uses this approach.
A hand splint that uses wrist extension to close the fingers. Used by some people with spinal cord injuries to grasp objects.
A rehabilitation brace that uses springs or elastic to help fingers move, usually to help open the hand after a stroke.
An artificial hand or hook driven by a cable connected to a harness, so a shoulder movement opens or closes it.
Brand names for an ultra-strong, very low-stretch fiber, sold as braided fishing line.
Thread made from a very strong, heat-resistant fiber. Stretches little and resists abrasion.
Measuring the device directly, for example the force needed to close the glove with a spring scale, instead of measuring a person’s effort.
Wearing the device with everything installed but disconnected (strings slack), to separate the effect of the assist from the effect of the hardware itself.
A 0–10 rating of how hard a task felt. Simple and quick, but subjective, so it pairs well with measured data.

pres.facts:
Grip strength in a pressurized glove drops to 46–58% of bare-hand strength (Mesloh et al.)
Most spacewalks last 5 to 8 hours
Artemis plans up to 24 hours of surface EVA per crewmember per week (Estep et al.)
Glove-related hand injuries have been reported throughout NASA’s history (McFarland et al.)
pres.prior:
NASA and GM’s Space Suit RoboGlove uses sensors and motors to pull tendons that help close the fingers
It reduced the effort to close the hand for more than half of test subjects (Madden et al.)
It also made opening the hand harder for many subjects, and it depends on power and electronics
This project asks whether a simpler, unpowered system can give some of the same help
pres.limitations:
Single test subject (the investigator)
Rubber bands approximate, but don’t reproduce, a pressurized glove
